Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The study explicitly states its aim to create an 'accessible and mobile casual game' (chunk_1, chunk_2) for blind and low-vision people, while also including a graphical user interface 'to encourage sighted users to play as well' (chunk_0, chunk_1, chunk_2). The goal was to explore 'how both blind and sighted users can share a common game experience' (chunk_1) and to enable them 'to enjoy the same level and quality of gameplay' (chunk_3). User feedback was sought on 'how fun and easy to use they found the game' (chunk_8), with the ultimate hope to make TapBeats 'truly accessible and fun' (chunk_9). This demonstrates a clear intention to prioritize both utility (accessibility) and fun from the outset for a diverse user group.

        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: TapBeats is described as a "musical rhythm game" and features modes like Memory Mode and Concert Mode where players must copy growing patterns of drum sounds or mimic rhythms to a background song, receiving a score. Career Mode further integrates these modes with specific objectives, all of which indicate a design with rigid rules, characteristic of a video game.

reasoning: The context describes various gameplay modes (Free Play, Memory Mode, Concert Mode, Studio Mode, Career Mode) which are all presented as single-player experiences where 'the player' or 'the user' interacts with the game. Furthermore, the text explicitly states that 'several multiplayer aspects to the game' are 'future features planned for TapBeats', indicating that the current design is entirely solo.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: TapBeats includes modes like Memory Mode and Concert Mode where the phone plays a pattern and the user mimics it, indicating a turn-based or sequential structure. However, it also features Free Play and Studio Mode, where users can press buttons or freestyle at any time, allowing for actions outside of a strict turn order. This combination best fits option (3).

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: TapBeats is described as a musical rhythm game, which inherently requires synchronous, real-time interaction (e.g., Memory Mode and Concert Mode where players mimic patterns to a beat). However, Studio Mode allows players to record and save their freestyle songs for later playback, introducing an asynchronous affordance.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The described game modes (Free Play, Memory Mode, Concert Mode, Studio Mode, Career Mode) are all single-player experiences, focusing on the individual player's interaction with the game system, such as mimicking patterns or freestyling. Modes like Memory Mode and Concert Mode involve the player attempting to correctly copy patterns and receiving a score, indicating a competitive element against the game's challenge. There is no mention of player-to-player collaboration or competition in the current design; multiplayer aspects are explicitly stated as a future feature. Therefore, interpreting 'competitive' as 'player versus game challenge' and noting the complete absence of player-to-player collaboration, the design is best categorized as entirely competitive.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The study aims for both blind and sighted users to share a common game experience and enjoy the same level and quality of gameplay, indicating a symmetrical core design. However, it employs different interaction methods, using audio cues, text-to-speech, and haptic feedback for blind users, and a graphical user interface for sighted users, which introduces an asymmetrical aspect to the design.
